title: 'Problems growing worse'; Two inmates died at Edmonton Institution in three days, causes of deaths unclear
article: Two inmates at Edmonton Institution have died in custody within days of each other, but authorities have not disclosed the causes of their deaths.

Evan Foureyes, 35, died on Feb. 21 while serving a four-year sentence since Jan. 14, 2022. Latto Sesay, 40, died on Feb. 23 while serving an eight-year, four-month and 13-day sentence since May 30, 2019. Both deaths were confirmed in the Correctional Service Canada (CSC) news releases, which said the inmates' next of kin have been notified and an internal review will be conducted, as per policy.
The Edmonton Police Service (EPS) said they investigated and determined that the deaths were non-criminal, but did not provide further details.

In a statement to Postmedia, CSC said it takes inmate deaths in its custody "very seriously" and in all cases of non-natural deaths in custody, police and the coroner are called to investigate. However, CSC cited privacy laws in declining to provide further details, deferring questions about the cause of death to the Chief Coroner's Office.

The Edmonton Institution, a maximum-security federal prison located in northeast Edmonton, has faced scrutiny in recent years over its conditions, with past reports citing issues such as overcrowding, staffing shortages, a toxic workplace culture, and concerns about inmate conditions. A 2017 report described the institution as operating under a "culture of fear," and in 2019, a survey revealed multiple allegations of sexual assault among staff.

The recent deaths at Edmonton Institution have sparked concerns about systemic issues within Canada's maximum-security prisons. In a statement to Postmedia, the Office of the Correctional Investigator (OCI) notes "any death in custody raises concerns about systemic issues, not just at Edmonton Institution, but across maximum-security institution as a whole."

Causes of deaths in custody are multifactorial and can include "violent incidents relating to conflicts between incompatible individuals, altercations between security threat groups, suicides, or overdoses."
"Rather than improving, the OCI's investigative teams have seen the problem growing worse year over year," the OCI ofcfi e said in the state - ment.

The Union of Canadian Correctional Officers (UCCO) has also long raised concerns about the working conditions at Edmonton Institution. James Bloomfield, prairies regional president with the UCCO, said while some deaths result from murders, others are due to "suicides that happen inside our institution," drug overdoses, or medical complications, which can be a heavy toll on correctional officers.

"When you have a loss of life in your workplace, whether it's an inmate or a staff member or anybody else, it still affects everybody," he said, noting officers are often first responders, performing CPR and managing traumatic situations.

Bloomfield also mentioned the dire state of mental health among correctional officers, saying "54 per cent of correctional officers will be diagnosed with a mental health injury in (their) fri st fvi e years." More support is needed, as more than 700 officers across the country are currently off work due to mental health injuries, he added.
One of the most pressing issues, he said, is the influx of drugs, largely brought in by drones, which fuels overdoses and violence.

"The biggest problem we have right now is drugs, and the introduction of drugs by drones into our institutions ... and that creates violence, that creates drug trade and a lot of the issues that we deal with that are very serious," he said, noting that is "something that we do need tremendous help in."
However, as of now, CSC is "very far behind, and we've had this issue for a large number of years. We're still far behind," Bloomfield said.

The OCI has also reported significant concerns regarding Edmonton Institution, consistent with national trends. In its latest report, the office found that maximum-security prisons "are highly restrictive and depriving to the point of undermining most other correctional objectives." Despite recommendations, there has been "a steady increase in use-of-force incidents, and rising numbers of self-inflicted injurious behaviour and attempted suicides."
The OCI has called for reforms, including better access to rehabilitation programs, increased employment training, and more oversight of correctional policies.
As investigations continue, both officers and incarcerated individuals continue to face an environment that is increasingly violent and mentally taxing.
